notes: Landmark PCO appeal on ECGD anti-bribery consultation challenge; Court of Appeal allowed appeal and directed cost-capped PCO.

enrichment.short_title: Corner House v DTI: protective costs order for ECGD bribery consultation challenge
key_facts: Corner House Research challenged ECGD's revision of anti-bribery disclosure requirements for export credit support, alleging unfair partial consultation with industry but not NGOs.
Beatson J granted an interim protective costs order (PCO) but Davis J refused a PCO for the substantive two-day judicial review hearing.
Corner House had only about £8,000 in unrestricted funds and said it would withdraw without costs protection.
The substantive judicial review was later disposed of by consent before merits were determined.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal application for permission to appeal with the appeal to follow on refusal of a protective costs order for a public law challenge.
enrichment.outcome: Permission to appeal granted; appeal allowed; PCO made with a cost-capping element following King v Telegraph Group; respondent ordered to pay appeal costs.
enrichment.ratio: A public interest challenger with real prospects of success and severely limited means may obtain a protective costs order where issues concern taxpayer-backed export credit, combating bribery, and compliance with published consultation policy; the CPAG merits threshold should not require near-certainty of success on complex judicial review.
legal_issues: Whether Davis J erred in refusing a PCO for the substantive judicial review hearing
Whether ECGD's consultation on anti-bribery procedure changes raised issues of general public importance
Whether Corner House had a real prospect of success on procedural unfairness and consultation policy grounds
Whether a cost-capped PCO was appropriate under King v Telegraph Group principles
linked_authorities: King v Telegraph Group Ltd [2004] EWCA Civ 613
R (Corner House Research) v Secretary of State for Trade and Industry [2004] EWHC 2774 (Admin)
R v Somerset County Council ex p Dixon [1998] Env LR 111

confidence.notes: Appellate reasoning on PCO principles and final order are explicit, though substantive JR merits were not adjudicated.

notes: Winding-up petition struck out where CVA and substantial pending arbitration outweighed creditor's special circumstances.

enrichment.short_title: Penwith v VP Developments: strike-out of council winding-up petition during CVA
key_facts: Penwith District Council presented a creditor's winding-up petition against VP Developments Ltd over disputed building contract debts.
The company had entered a company voluntary arrangement and was pursuing a substantial Alverton arbitration claim worth over £367,000.
Earlier arbitrations had produced costs orders in the council's favour estimated at £100,000-£150,000, but those costs were unassessed and likely to be set off against any Alverton award.
The council argued its post-CVA status and possible director claims were special circumstances warranting winding up.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Cross-applications on a creditor's winding-up petition and the company's application to strike out or stay the petition.
enrichment.outcome: Winding-up petition struck out; no sufficient special circumstances to allow the petition to proceed.
enrichment.ratio: Where a company is in a CVA and a serious substantial arbitration remains live, allowing a creditor's winding-up petition to proceed would likely terminate that process and penalise the company for entering the CVA; speculative liquidator investigations do not constitute compelling special circumstances.
legal_issues: Whether the council's winding-up petition should be struck out or stayed
Whether post-CVA creditor status and unassessed costs orders amounted to special circumstances
Whether pursuit of the petition was an abuse of process
Effect of pending arbitration on winding-up discretion
linked_authorities: In Re N T Gallaher & Son Ltd [2002] 1 WLR 2380

confidence.notes: Discretionary strike-out reasoning and final order are clearly stated.

notes: Long Sharia-compliant fund trial; Moore-Bick J found UBK negligent on lease advice but deferred final liability and quantum.

enrichment.short_title: Riyad Bank v Ahli United Bank: negligence in Sharia-compliant lease fund advice
key_facts: Riyad Bank and RBE London sued United Bank of Kuwait over advice given on the IIBU II Sharia-compliant equipment lease fund.
Claimants alleged UBK negligently failed to scrutinise asset managers' over-optimistic ERVs and renewal assumptions when recommending lease purchases.
The Fund sought damages for negligent misstatement; Riyad Bank also pursued breach of the Technical Services Agreement after buying out investors.
UBK argued contractual termination by notice did not waive claims and disputed direct tortious duties to the Fund.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court trial on liability in a large commercial claim concerning negligent investment advice on an Islamic finance fund.
enrichment.outcome: Court found UBK failed to carry out independent analysis of ERVs and renewal assumptions and breached its duty of care, but further directions were required because final liability and quantum could not yet be determined across the portfolio.
enrichment.ratio: A technical services consultant advising a Sharia-compliant fund owes a duty to take reasonable care in evaluating lease residual values and suitability; breach must be assessed lease-by-lease, recovery is limited to the difference between price paid and actual value, and contractual notice to terminate does not waive damages for prior breaches absent clear waiver.
legal_issues: Whether UBK owed the Fund a duty of care in negligent misstatement
Whether UBK failed to exercise reasonable skill in analysing ERVs and renewal assumptions
Whether Riyad Bank could recover under the Technical Services Agreement after novation
Whether notice terminating the agreement waived negligence claims
linked_authorities: Hedley Byrne & Co Ltd v Heller & Partners Ltd [1964] AC 465
Henderson v Merrett Syndicates Ltd [1995] 2 AC 145
Alfred McAlpine Construction Ltd v Panatown Ltd [2001] 1 AC 518

confidence.notes: Core duty-of-care and breach findings are explicit, but final dispositions on individual leases and quantum remained for further trial.

notes: Leading school uniform and Article 9 judgment; Court of Appeal allowed appeal and granted three declarations.

enrichment.short_title: SB v Denbigh High School: jilbab, school uniform and Article 9 ECHR
key_facts: SB, a Muslim pupil, wished to wear a jilbab rather than the school's approved shalwar kameeze uniform at Denbigh High School in Luton.
The headteacher and governors excluded her for refusing to comply with the uniform policy.
The school served a diverse Muslim community and had sought to accommodate differing religious dress views through its uniform options.
Bennett J dismissed the judicial review, but the Court of Appeal held Article 9(1) was engaged without deciding Article 9(2) justification.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from Administrative Court refusal of judicial review of a school's uniform and exclusion decision.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; three declarations granted that the school unlawfully excluded SB, unlawfully denied her right to manifest her religion, and unlawfully denied access to suitable education.
enrichment.ratio: Article 9 protects minority religious dress choices such as the jilbab even where a school offers other Muslim-compliant uniform options; a school may not treat engagement of Article 9 as dependent on majority practice, and exclusion for religious dress without a proper Article 9(2) analysis violates Convention rights.
legal_issues: Whether SB was excluded from school because of her religious dress
Whether Article 9(1) was engaged by the uniform policy
Whether any limitation was justified under Article 9(2)
Whether the school unlawfully denied access to suitable education
linked_authorities: A v Headteacher and Governors of Lord Grey School [2004] EWCA Civ 382
R (SB) v Denbigh High School [2004] EWHC 1389 (Admin)

confidence.notes: Appellate declarations and Article 9 reasoning are detailed and clearly reasoned.

notes: VAT zero-rating interim relief appeal; main appeal dismissed on CPR 25.7 but costs cross-appeal allowed.

enrichment.short_title: Teleos v Customs and Excise: interim VAT payment during ECJ reference
key_facts: Teleos challenged HMRC's decision that mobile phone exports did not qualify for zero-rated VAT, with about £1.5 million assessed and over £1 million set off against input tax credits.
Moses J referred interpretation questions to the ECJ, with a decision unlikely before 2006.
Teleos sought interim payment of about £529,000 plus costs to avoid winding up while awaiting the reference.
The Commissioners cross-appealed against an adverse costs order on the interim application.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal and cross-appeal from refusal of interim monetary relief in VAT judicial review proceedings pending an ECJ reference.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; cross-appeal allowed; Commissioners awarded costs of the application; court ordered an interim payment of £15,000; permission to appeal refused.
enrichment.ratio: An application for interim payment of disputed VAT must satisfy CPR 25.7 and cannot be reframed as general interim relief or supported by an inherent jurisdiction to order payment before liability is established; EC law does not create a freestanding interim payment remedy where domestic conditions are unmet.
legal_issues: Whether Teleos was entitled to interim payment pending an ECJ reference
Whether CPR 25.7 or the court's inherent jurisdiction applied
Whether EC VAT law required interim payment despite unmet CPR conditions
Whether costs of the interim application should follow the event
linked_authorities: Capital One Developments Ltd v Customs and Excise Commissioners [2002] EWHC 197 (Ch)
LAMIT v Customs & Excise Commissioners [2003] EWHC 2766 (Ch)
Business Research & Development NV v Belgium [1997] ECR I-7281

confidence.notes: Appellate reasoning on CPR 25.7 and costs is explicit; final order also records a limited £15,000 interim payment.

notes: Gypsy Green Belt enforcement challenge; Secretary of State decision quashed over misapplied search-for-sites evidence.

enrichment.short_title: Simmons v SoS: gypsy caravan site in Green Belt and alternative site searches

statutes_considered.title: Caravan Sites and Control of Development Act 1960

key_facts: Mr Simmons, an Irish traveller gypsy, appealed against enforcement of residential caravan use on Green Belt land at Halstead, Kent.
The inspector recommended allowing the appeal, finding very special circumstances including unmet gypsy accommodation need.
The Secretary of State called the appeal in and upheld the enforcement notice, citing lack of evidence of searches for alternative sites.
The claimant argued the Secretary of State misapplied Circular 1/94 and ignored evidence of searches and site unavailability.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of the Secretary of State's decision on a called-in Green Belt enforcement appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Secretary of State's decision quashed; further relief to be determined on submissions.
enrichment.ratio: A gypsy in a Green Belt enforcement appeal is not subject to a standalone evidential burden to prove searches across the county; where an inspector found no alternative sites available, the Secretary of State could not properly reject the appeal merely for unclear evidence of pre-purchase searches or failure to consult planning authorities when that evidence did not affect site availability.
legal_issues: Whether gypsies must prove searches for alternative sites in Green Belt cases
Whether the Secretary of State erred in treating lack of search evidence as decisive
Whether Circular 1/94 imposed an evidential obligation on gypsies
Whether the Secretary of State could depart from the inspector on Green Belt harm without a site visit

confidence.notes: Central quashing ground on search evidence is clearly reasoned, though some subsidiary planning grounds were rejected.

notes: Injunction granted restraining £1.175m estate agents' winding-up petition over disputed Kensington Palace Gardens commission.

enrichment.short_title: Favermead v Savills: injunction over disputed £1.175m agency commission
key_facts: Three joint selling agents claimed £1,175,000 commission after the sale of 18-19 Kensington Palace Gardens for $105 million to Laken Properties.
Favermead originally retained the agents but later sold through Corfiducia Anstalt; the agency letter required payment if an introduced purchaser completed.
Agents served a statutory demand and threatened a winding-up petition against Favermead.
Favermead disputed liability, arguing implied terms required the agents to be the effective cause of sale and that post-November 2001 circumstances changed the agency relationship.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Interlocutory application for an injunction restraining presentation of a winding-up petition based on a disputed statutory demand.
enrichment.outcome: Injunction granted restraining presentation of the winding-up petition.
enrichment.ratio: Where there is a real and substantial dispute about liability for a large agent's commission, especially on whether introducers must be the effective cause of sale and how changed ownership affected the agency, the court should restrain a winding-up petition rather than allow disputed commercial claims to be resolved by compulsory liquidation.
legal_issues: Whether Favermead genuinely disputed the commission debt on substantial grounds
Whether the agency agreement required the agents to be effective cause of the sale
Effect of Corfiducia replacing Favermead as vendor after November 2001
Whether an implied term limited commission to introductions that actually procured the sale
linked_authorities: Cooper & Co v Fairview Estates Investments Ltd [1987] 1 EGLR 18

confidence.notes: Interlocutory dispute-of-debt reasoning is clear though commission merits remain untried.

notes: Attorney General reference on unduly lenient community order for large-scale credit card cloning conspiracy.

enrichment.short_title: AG Ref 141 of 2004: unduly lenient sentence for credit card cloning conspiracy
key_facts: The offender pleaded guilty to conspiracy to defraud by facilitating cloned credit and debit cards over about two years.
Police found a card-cloning factory, indent machines, compromised card numbers and losses of about £150,000.
He was sentenced to a 220-hour community punishment order as neither instigator nor principal organiser.
The co-accused Charles absconded before trial.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Attorney General's reference under section 36 of the Criminal Justice Act 1988 alleging an unduly lenient sentence.
enrichment.outcome: Reference granted; community order quashed; substituted sentence of 15 months' imprisonment, with surrender to custody permitted the following day.
enrichment.ratio: Large-scale persistent credit card cloning causing substantial loss warranted a sentence of about two-and-a-half to three years; a community order was unduly lenient, though double jeopardy, partial completion of the community order, and delay justified reducing the substituted term to 15 months.
legal_issues: Whether a 220-hour community punishment order was unduly lenient
Appropriate sentencing range for facilitators in large-scale card cloning conspiracies
Application of double jeopardy principles on Attorney General references
Weight to be given to partial completion of the original community order
linked_authorities: Attorney General's Reference (R v Ranganathan) [2004] 2 Cr App R(S) 337
Attorney General's Reference (Gardner and Samuel) [2003] EWCA Crim 2633

confidence.notes: Facts, sentencing range analysis and substituted sentence are all clearly recorded.

notes: Judicial review dismissed; hospital order with restriction upheld for unfit defendant with escalating paranoid schizophrenia.

enrichment.short_title: Jones v Isleworth Crown Court: restriction order after unfitness finding

statutes_considered.title: Criminal Procedure (Insanity and Unfitness to Plead) Act 1991

key_facts: The claimant faced burglary and attempted burglary charges and was found unfit to plead after a long history of offending.
A jury found he committed the acts alleged; the Crown Court made a hospital order with restriction under Schedule 1 of the 1991 Act.
He suffered paranoid schizophrenia with command hallucinations and a history of drug misuse and escalating violence.
Psychiatric evidence was mixed, but the judge concluded there was a risk of serious harm including physical violence and burglary to fund drugs.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of a Crown Court disposal under the insanity and unfitness statutory scheme.
enrichment.outcome: Application for judicial review dismissed; restriction order upheld as amply warranted by the evidence.
enrichment.ratio: On disposal after unfitness, a judge may impose a restriction order where future risk of serious harm is inferred from escalating violence, command hallucinations and drug abuse even if past offences were not all at the highest level of violence; the judge is not bound by psychiatric opinion and must assess future risk.
legal_issues: Whether there was evidence supporting a finding of risk of serious harm
Whether harm must be limited to physical injury under Birch principles
Whether the judge was bound by Dr Omar's psychiatric opinion
Lawfulness of a restriction order under Schedule 1 of the 1991 Act
linked_authorities: R v Birch [1990] 90 Cr App R 78

confidence.notes: Issue and dismissal on evidential sufficiency are clearly reasoned.

notes: Short procedural judgment on anonymous immigration claim, litigator authorisation and costs against legal advisers.

enrichment.short_title: Victoria Eleison v Home Secretary: procedural orders on anonymous immigration claim
key_facts: The claimants, described as Musical Group Victoria Eleison, brought judicial review against the Home Secretary.
No application was made for a section 28(2)(c) direction and Hughes J doubted one would have been appropriate.
Counsel Mr Offeh withdrew from the application during the hearing.
The court made procedural orders requiring individual identification, authorised litigator confirmation, and show-cause steps as to costs against African Legal Advisory Services.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Procedural hearing in judicial review concerning litigator authorisation, anonymity and costs against legal advisers.
enrichment.outcome: No section 28 direction made; claim to stand dismissed in 28 days unless claimants identified themselves and confirmed authorised representation; African Legal Advisory Services ordered to show cause why they should not pay costs.
enrichment.ratio: An immigration judicial review cannot proceed indefinitely without individually identified claimants and written confirmation from authorised litigators of their intention to pursue the claim; where representatives withdraw, the court may impose time-limited dismissal and require legal advisers to show cause on costs.
legal_issues: Whether a section 28(2)(c) direction should be made
Consequences of withdrawal of counsel and failure to identify claimants
Whether the claim should be dismissed for want of proper authorisation
Whether African Legal Advisory Services should be liable for costs
index_terms: section 28 Courts and Legal Services Act

confidence.notes: Very short procedural order with clear dispositions, but little substantive immigration reasoning is recorded.
